groups.name: Lumbar spinal stenosis
items: Thigh pain after 30 s lumbar extension
groups.explanation: Stenosis narrows the canal and foramina. Extension narrows them further and flexion opens them, so patients lean on carts and feel better sitting. Leg symptoms with walking that ease with flexion, not just with standing still, point to neurogenic rather than vascular claudication.

groups.name: Lumbar disc herniation
items: Pain worse with cough or sneeze
groups.explanation: SLR is sensitive for radiculopathy from a herniated disc, and crossed SLR is specific. Valsalva raises intrathecal pressure and aggravates the irritated root. Radicular pain usually follows a dermatome and runs below the knee.

groups.name: SI joint dysfunction
groups.explanation: Laslett's cluster uses five provocation tests: distraction, thigh thrust, compression, sacral thrust, and Gaenslen. Three or more positive tests make SIJ pain more likely. The Fortin finger sign, where the patient points to just below the PSIS, is a supporting clue.

groups.name: Hip osteoarthritis
groups.explanation: Sutlive's cluster includes painful squatting, a painful scour, and limited internal rotation. Hip OA usually follows a capsular pattern, with IR lost first. Morning stiffness that clears within an hour separates OA from inflammatory arthritis.

groups.name: Full-thickness rotator cuff tear
groups.explanation: Lag signs and drop arm test whether the tendon can hold a position, not just whether it hurts. A lag means the tendon has lost continuity. Hornblower's points to infraspinatus/teres minor, and lift-off points to subscapularis.

groups.name: Subacromial pain syndrome
groups.explanation: These tests compress the subacromial space during elevation and rotation. A painful arc that eases above 120° is typical. Relief after a subacromial anesthetic injection (the Neer test) supports a subacromial source.

groups.name: Adhesive capsulitis
items: Active and passive ROM equally lost
groups.explanation: The capsule contracts, so passive motion is lost as much as active motion, with external rotation hit hardest. Diabetes is a major risk factor. Imaging is usually normal, which helps rule out glenohumeral OA, the other condition with a capsular pattern.

groups.name: SLAP / labral tear
groups.explanation: The superior labrum anchors the long head of biceps. Tests that load the biceps anchor (O'Brien, Biceps load II) or grind the labrum (Crank) provoke symptoms, and mechanical clicking with overhead motion is common. No single test is definitive, so use them together.

groups.name: Posterior canal BPPV
items: Rolling over in bed triggers it
groups.explanation: Loose otoconia in the posterior canal cause brief vertigo when the head moves relative to gravity. Dix-Hallpike provokes upbeating, torsional nystagmus after a short latency, and it fades with repeated testing. Treat with canalith repositioning (Epley).

groups.name: Vestibular neuritis
groups.explanation: Inflammation of the vestibular nerve causes a sudden, ongoing loss of input from one side. The head impulse test shows a corrective saccade toward the bad side, and nystagmus beats away from it in one direction only. Hearing is spared.

groups.name: Central cause (posterior circulation stroke)
items: Normal head impulse in acute vertigo
groups.explanation: HINTS is dangerous when any one of these appears: a normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, or a positive test of skew. In acute vestibular syndrome, HINTS outperforms early MRI. Add any cerebellar sign and this needs emergency referral.

groups.name: Ménière's disease
groups.explanation: Endolymphatic hydrops causes recurring attacks of vertigo together with ear symptoms. Episodes last longer than BPPV and shorter than neuritis, and hearing loss, fullness, and tinnitus set it apart from the other three.
